client: I failed my calculus final last week, and I just can't stop thinking about it. It's like this constant voice in my head telling me I'm not smart enough to be in my major, that maybe I picked the wrong path entirely. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, because the grade is already there and it's not going away.
therapist: It makes complete sense that this is weighing so heavily on you — a setback like this can feel like it says something permanent and defining about who you are, and that constant inner voice can be exhausting to carry. You're right that the grade itself won't change, but I'm curious about that voice telling you you're "not smart enough" — what evidence does it lean on, and is there any evidence in your life that might push back against it? What does your story look like *beyond* this one exam?

client: I mean, yeah, I passed my other classes this semester, and I did okay in pre-calc last year. But it feels like calculus is the thing that actually matters for my major, so those other wins just don't feel like they count the same way. It's like my brain keeps saying "sure, but this is the one that really tests whether you belong here."
therapist: It's really insightful that you can already see the pattern — your mind is essentially moving the goalposts, discounting the wins and elevating this one result as the ultimate "belonging test," which is a very common but painful thinking trap called **discounting the positive**. It's worth gently questioning: who decided that this single exam gets to be the sole judge of whether you belong in your major — is that a rule you'd apply to a friend in the same situation? What do you think *actually* determines whether someone belongs in a field they care about?

client: I know logically I wouldn't tell a friend they don't belong just because they failed one exam, and I can see what you're doing with that question. But it feels different when it's me, like the rules just don't apply the same way — I hold myself to this standard that I can't really explain or justify. I guess what actually determines belonging is probably more about persistence and effort over time, but right now that feels like a nice idea that doesn't really touch how bad I feel.
therapist: You've just named something really profound — that you *know* the more compassionate logic, but the feeling hasn't caught up yet, and that gap between knowing and feeling is real and valid, not a sign that you're doing something wrong. Feelings often need more than one good argument to shift; they need time, small experiences, and gentle repetition of a different story. I'm wondering, what would one small act of persistence look like for you this week — something that lets you *show yourself*, not just tell yourself, that you're still in the fight?

client: I guess I could try going to the professor's office hours to understand where I went wrong on the exam, but honestly that feels kind of terrifying — like I'd be walking in and confirming to them that I really don't get it. There's this fear that if I ask for help, it just proves I'm not cut out for this, which I know probably sounds backwards. I'm not sure I can make myself do it this week, it feels like a lot.
therapist: That fear makes a lot of sense — there's a deeply ingrained story that asking for help is an admission of inadequacy, when in reality most professors see students who seek help as engaged and committed, not incompetent. It's also worth noticing that the very thing that feels like "proof you don't belong" might actually be one of the most belonging-affirming actions you could take. What do you imagine the *best possible version* of that office hours visit could look like — not the scary version, but the one where it actually goes okay?

client: I guess in the best case, the professor is just kind of neutral about it, explains what I got wrong, and I actually understand something I didn't before. Maybe I even leave feeling slightly less lost about the material. But I keep coming back to this worry that even if it goes fine on the outside, I'll still walk out of there feeling like a fraud, like the good outcome won't actually stick with me emotionally the way the bad feelings do.
therapist: You've just described something really important — that you're almost pre-emptively discounting the good outcome before it even happens, which shows how much that inner critic wants to protect its story about you. But notice that you *did* imagine a genuinely okay version of events, which means some part of you believes it's possible, and that part deserves just as much airtime as the fear. I'm curious — what if the goal of going wasn't to walk out feeling completely "fixed," but just to collect one small piece of evidence that you can show up for yourself even when it's hard?

client: That framing actually helps a little — like, lowering the bar from "feel better" to just "show up" makes it feel slightly less impossible. But I think part of me is scared that even showing up won't be enough, that I'll do the hard thing and still feel just as lost and alone with it afterward, and then what? It's like I'm worried that trying and it not fixing anything would almost be worse than not trying at all.
therapist: That fear of trying and still feeling lost is so deeply human — it's actually your mind trying to protect you from disappointment, but the cost is that it keeps you stuck in a place that already hurts. It's worth sitting with this: right now, without trying, you're already feeling lost and alone with it — so in some ways, the worst case you're afraid of is already where you are, and showing up at least adds one small piece of new information to your story. What do you think it would mean about you *as a person* if you tried and still felt uncertain afterward — would that really be proof that you don't belong, or might it just mean that healing moves slower than one office visit?

client: When you put it that way, I can see the logic — I'm already in the painful place, so trying doesn't actually make the floor lower than it already is. But I think what scares me is less about the outcome and more about the loneliness of it, like even if I go and it goes okay, I'll still walk back to my dorm alone with all these feelings and no one to really process it with. It's almost like the exam failure is tangled up with this bigger feeling that I'm just kind of navigating all of this by myself.
therapist: Thank you for trusting me with that — because what you just named feels like the heart of it, that the exam is painful but the loneliness underneath it may be what's making it so hard to bear. That feeling of navigating life without someone to really process it with is its own real, separate ache that deserves attention, not just the calculus grade. I'm wondering — is there anyone in your life right now, even someone unexpected, who might be more available to walk alongside you in this than you currently let them?

client: There's maybe one person — a classmate I've studied with a few times who seems genuinely nice — but I haven't really let it go beyond surface-level study stuff because I'm always worried about being too much or coming across as needy. I guess I keep people at a distance without really realizing I'm doing it, and then I end up feeling alone and wondering why. It's kind of uncomfortable to see that pattern so clearly right now.
therapist: It takes real courage to see that pattern so clearly, and the fact that it feels uncomfortable is actually a sign of genuine self-awareness, not something to be ashamed of. There's something worth gently questioning in that word "needy" — because wanting connection and someone to process hard things with isn't neediness, it's just being human, and that classmate who seems genuinely nice might actually welcome the chance to know you more fully. What do you think might happen if you let just a small amount of the real stuff show with them — not everything at once, just one honest moment?

client: I think maybe nothing catastrophic would happen if I let a little bit of the real stuff show, like mentioning I've been stressed about the exam or something small like that. But there's this voice that says if I do that and they pull away or get weird about it, it'll just confirm that I'm better off keeping to myself. I guess I'm realizing this session that a lot of my loneliness might actually be something I'm partly creating, and that's a hard thing to sit with.
therapist: Sitting with that kind of realization — that we've had a hand in our own pain — takes real honesty and courage, and it's important to hold it with compassion rather than as another reason to criticize yourself, because you built those walls for good reasons at some point. And you're right that there's a risk someone might pull away, but you've also shown today that you're capable of real, meaningful connection — you've let quite a bit of the real stuff show right here in this conversation. I'm wondering, what does it tell you about yourself that despite all these protective instincts, some part of you keeps reaching out — here today, and maybe toward that classmate — rather than giving up entirely?

client: I guess it tells me that some part of me hasn't completely given up, even when it feels like I have, which is a strange thing to realize. I don't know, maybe there's something stubborn in me that keeps looking for connection even when I'm simultaneously pushing it away. I'm not ready to call that a strength yet, but I can at least acknowledge it's there.
therapist: That stubborn, reaching part of you that keeps showing up even when another part is pushing connection away — that's not a small thing, and you don't have to call it a strength yet, but I'd gently invite you to notice that it's the same part that brought you here today, that imagined a best-case office hours visit, and that's already thinking about being a little more real with your classmate. You've done a lot of honest, courageous work in this conversation, and I don't want that to get lost in the shuffle of everything that still feels hard. As you carry all of this with you this week, what's one thing — however small — that you want to remember from today?
